brief.summary: A study and deadline planner that a community college gives every student in its required first-semester College Success course, with built-in walkthroughs and help for students who have never had to organize a term's workload themselves.
brief.user: Jaylen Brooks, 19, a first-generation college student enrolled in four courses at a community college while working 20 hours a week at a grocery store. He's comfortable with phones and social apps but has never used a planner. His College Success instructor, Ms. Ortega, requires everyone to have their term set up by the Week 2 check-in.
brief.moment: It's Sunday evening of Week 1. Jaylen has finished the first few setup steps: he added his four courses and entered his work shifts. Now he's stuck adding his Intro to Psychology syllabus. The class assigns a reading every Tuesday and Thursday, and he can't figure out how to enter repeating readings without typing 30 of them by hand, or whether a 'reading' is the same thing as an 'assignment'. He wants a quick answer at the point where he's confused, without losing what he's already entered, and he wants to see what's left on Ms. Ortega's checklist before the Tuesday check-in.
brief.data: Term: Fall 2026, Aug 24 – Dec 11, 16 weeks. Jaylen's courses: PSY 101 (TTh 9:30, Dr. Kim), ENG 101 (MW 11:00), MATH 095 (MWF 8:00, plus online homework due Sundays), COLL 100 College Success (Th 1:00, Ms. Ortega). Work shifts: Fri 4–10 pm, Sat and Sun 10 am–4 pm. Partly entered PSY 101 syllabus: 30 readings (Ch. 1–15, two sessions each), 4 exams (Sep 17, Oct 15, Nov 12, Dec 10), 3 short papers. Ms. Ortega's 7-step setup checklist, with 3 done (add courses, add work, set a weekly study block) and 4 to go (import every syllabus, set exam reminders, plan a week, share with your instructor). Help content: 26 short how-to articles, a 'repeating items' walkthrough, and drop-in hours for the campus tutoring center's peer coaches (Mon–Thu 10 am–6 pm). Jaylen's progress: the intro walkthrough was skipped at step 3 of 6.

Build it as a working web app, opened in the state that person would see at that moment. No backend: use realistic mock data (no lorem ipsum, no placeholder names), and make the interactive parts actually work client-side.

Use whatever framework and tooling you like. When you're done there must be a static production build in ./out with ./out/index.html as the entry point. It will be served from the root of a plain static file server (no rewrites, no server code) and viewed in a desktop browser at 1440×900.
